name: Iran

position.summary: Iran entered the week under a layered set of pressures. A US diplomatic response had reached Tehran through Qatari mediators, even though President Trump had publicly rejected the earlier Iranian proposal, keeping the channel alive. In the military dimension, Washington was deploying a third carrier strike group and thousands of additional troops toward the region, while Trump acknowledged that some munitions stocks were low and floated the idea of larger strikes after the November midterms. Domestically, the rial sat at record lows, the central bank was selling dollars to prop up the currency, and September oil loading had been minimal under blockade and sanctions pressure. New 'Operation Economic Outcast' sanctions targeted auto, rail, and aviation sectors. The regime was blocking SIM cards, freezing bank accounts, and tightening digital surveillance. Two incidents—the FlyDubai copilot attack and the RAF Fairford plot—gave Washington and London potential casus belli arguments. Iran had captured a US underwater drone and was using it as propaganda. The US was withdrawing forces from Iraq. Proxy activity from the Houthis and Iraqi militias was intensifying, and Iranian leadership was internally debating whether to threaten a NPT exit.

key_events.event: Iran received a US diplomatic response through Qatari mediators despite Trump's public rejection of the earlier proposal.
The US deployed a third carrier strike group and thousands of troops toward the region while Trump admitted low munitions stocks.
The rial fell to record lows and the central bank began selling dollars to support the currency.
The FlyDubai copilot attack and RAF Fairford plot gave the US and UK potential casus belli arguments against Iran.
The regime intensified SIM-card blocks, bank-account freezes, and digital surveillance of activists and merchants.

emoji_reasons: Qatari and Omani mediators were actively pushing both sides toward a trust-building arrangement around the Strait of Hormuz.
The US was deploying a third carrier group and additional troops while Iran readied missile batteries and drone defenses.
The rial was at record lows and the central bank was selling dollars to slow the slide as import costs surged.

naive_forecast.summary: The most likely path, taken at face value, is a week of managed tension with no major break. Iran publicly acknowledges the US response and Qatari mediators schedule a follow-up technical session in Doha. A Houthi missile or drone hits a commercial vessel in the Red Sea or Gulf, and Iran credits the 'resistance' for the attack. The rial breaks its previous record low and the central bank announces a new dollar-sale operation, while bazaar merchants close in protest. Digital authorities freeze at least two hundred SIM cards and bank accounts linked to critical voices. By week's end, Iran and US officials jointly announce a seven-day monitored oil-shipping corridor through Hormuz as a small trust-building test, with a temporary sanctions waiver as the quid pro quo. No full-scale strike, no NPT exit, no mass uprising—the regime buys time, shows strength, and keeps the economy from tipping.

statements.text: Iran's Foreign Ministry issues a public statement confirming it received and is 'examining' the US proposal delivered via Qatari mediators, and Qatari officials schedule a follow-up technical session in Doha within the week.

A Houthi missile or drone strikes a commercial vessel or coastal energy facility in the Red Sea or Gulf, and Iranian state television broadcasts the attack as a 'resistance action' while denying direct IRGC involvement.

Iran's central bank announces a new dollar-sale operation or revised exchange-rate mechanism after the rial breaks its previous record low, and Tehran's Grand Bazaar merchants hold a one-day closure in protest.

Iranian digital authorities revoke or freeze at least 200 SIM cards and bank accounts belonging to activists, merchants, or university students who posted critical content, and the regime's IT minister announces 'surgical' measures against 'cyber-dissidents.'

Iran and US officials jointly announce a seven-day monitored oil-shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz as a trust-building test, with the US granting a temporary sanctions waiver on Iranian oil exports.

crystal_forecast.summary: Weighing the full distribution of outcomes, the crystal reading elevates the minority-probability scenarios that the naive headline case underweights. The 30 to 40 percent band for a limited US or Israeli airstrike, triggered specifically by confirmed FlyDubai or RAF Fairford evidence, becomes a genuine live risk rather than a footnote. The 15 to 25 percent chance that talks stall entirely on the nuclear-versus-sanctions sequencing question means the week could end with no document signed at all. The 10 to 20 percent Hormuz incident scenario, in which a mine or naval confrontation forces a US convoy system and Brent crude spikes above 110 dollars, is a tail risk with outsized impact. The rial devaluation and a Majlis capital-controls bill are still the base case, but the crystal reading pairs them with a higher probability of a visible parliamentary showdown with bazaar merchants. The overall picture is the same managed tension, but with sharper edges on the downside.
crystal_forecast.reasoning: The naive reading takes the text's single most-likely narrative: the fragile trust-building test begins, talks proceed, one proxy hit occurs, the rial weakens, digital crackdowns tighten, and a small confidence measure is announced. The crystal reading instead weights the text's full probability table: the 30 to 40 percent limited-strike band, the 15 to 25 percent talks-stall band, and the 10 to 20 percent serious-Hormuz-incident band are treated as scenarios with enough probability to shape the expected outcome. The FlyDubai and RAF Fairford triggers, which the text calls 'not just side notes,' become the most probable path into a limited strike because they give Washington a casus belli that avoids the political cost of a Hormuz war. The crystal reading also adjusts the Hormuz confidence-measure probability downward, noting it is conditional on 'if things are calm,' and introduces the Majlis capital-controls bill as a specific observable that the text's domestic section implies but does not explicitly predict.

statements.text: The US Department of Defense confirms a limited retaliatory airstrike on Iranian IRGC drone production sites or Quds Force cells after confirming evidence linking Iran to the FlyDubai copilot attack, with Washington citing the incident as casus belli alongside the RAF Fairford plot.

Iran's Foreign Ministry publicly suspends technical talks and rebukes Qatari mediators in a written statement, citing the US demand to return IAEA inspectors to Natanz before any sanctions relief as the sticking point, ending the week with no document signed.

Iran's central bank announces a 40 percent devaluation of the official rial rate or introduces a dual-currency trading window, and the rial closes the week at a new all-time low against the US dollar.

A naval confrontation or unexploded ordnance incident in the Strait of Hormuz forces the US Fifth Fleet to impose a temporary escort convoy system for oil tankers, and Brent crude trades above 110 US dollars per barrel at least once during the week.

Iran's Majlis votes to pass a new 'economic-war response' bill imposing capital controls, import licensing requirements, and mandatory price ceilings, and bazaar merchants in Tehran hold a two-day sit-in outside the parliament building in opposition.

display.headline: Iran balances Hormuz diplomacy, proxy pressure, and economic pain
emoji_reasons: The central prediction was a fragile Qatari-brokered trust-building test around the Strait of Hormuz.
Maritime tension in Hormuz and Houthi attacks on shipping were the main military flashpoint for the week.
Worsening currency collapse and inflation were the dominant domestic storyline.
display.tldr: Qatari mediators push a fragile Hormuz trust-building test while US military posture intensifies and Houthi proxy attacks keep pressure on Gulf shipping. The rial slides further, digital crackdowns tighten, and FlyDubai evidence looms as a strike trigger. No full-scale war, no clean deal—managed attrition.
